IntroPage.629vqpym: Hi, if you have no idea what <Vocab>Ethereum</Vocab>, <Vocab>blockchains</Vocab>, and <Vocab>smart contracts</Vocab> are, this is for you!
IntroPage.3ectbee7: This is a series of articles that tries to explain the basics of blockchain in a simplified way. I do my best to avoid heavy math or programming jargon, but there will be some new words and ideas. I try to use real-world examples when possible to help bridge the gap.
IntroPage.622va93a: (For all the experts in the room, just enjoy the animations.)
IntroPage.qah5lu5d: Along the way, we'll cover how blockchains:
IntroPage.fryusi0v: Let us send and receive money 24/7
IntroPage.doshlf6s: What is Ethereum ? Ethereum is a <Vocab>blockchain network</Vocab> for <Vocab>sending money</Vocab> and <Vocab>running apps</Vocab>
IntroPage.f840xv5l: In general, a <Vocab>network</Vocab> is a group of connected things, like a social network. As long as something is in the network, you can reach it. Just like how on the Facebook network, you can send a message to anyone as long as they have an account.
IntroPage.ikdtibbf: I know we didn't define <Vocab>blockchain</Vocab> yet, don't worry, we'll get to it.
IntroPage.a9hclw7n: Like a social media network, you'll need an <Vocab>account</Vocab> to get started using Ethereum. An account will let you receive <Vocab>money</Vocab>. You can receive many types of digital assets with your account.
IntroPage.9t1nke57: Let's give you a test account to get started:
IntroPage.ua9t9jjq: Every account has a unique ID, called an <Vocab>address</Vocab>.
IntroPage.x9so2of4: Just like how an email address lets you receive emails on the internet, your Ethereum address lets you receive ETH on the Ethereum network.
IntroPage.b20b6d5j: What is ETH ? ETH is the native currency of the Ethereum network. Like Bitcoin, it's another digital currency that you can trade or transfer.
IntroPage.kko6aqms: Here, let's give you 1 (simulated) ETH to get started below.
IntroPage.0cg0yr72: Now that you have some ETH, you can send it around to other people.
IntroPage.86yfogoc: Let's give you some simulated friends to send money to.
IntroPage.yn7s495v: Now try sending them some ETH!
IntroPage.sk87b2kb: Nice! After sending ETH, we get the pop-up below. What does it mean ?
IntroPage.cg6aycpv: Once it turns green, your send transaction has been <Vocab>confirmed</Vocab>. This lets you know that it was successful, i.e. that it went through.
IntroPage.40aeb9sj: Sending money on Ethereum isn't instant. It's faster than a bank transfer (no need to wait 1-2 business days), but it's also a little slower than Venmo or Zelle.
IntroPage.fr0x2iz1: Specifically, on Ethereum, it takes <Vocab>up to 12 seconds</Vocab> to complete a transaction.
IntroPage.tdx91hk9: Does this mean we can only take one action on Ethereum every 12 seconds ? If so, that would be inconvenient.
IntroPage.ljkxis6h: What if we have to send money to multiple people ? Do we need to send first to Alice, wait 12 seconds, then send to Bob, wait, and so on ?
IntroPage.c9q8j8vo: On Ethereum, we can send out multiple transactions to different accounts. Then, in around 12 seconds, they'll all happen one after another in quick succession.
IntroPage.8nvl76pp: How does that work ? Here's an example.
IntroPage.x3uk9e0n: Imagine that we're at a train station, and we want to deliver some packages to the next stop. If we have multiple packages to deliver, we can still put them all on the same train, and they'll all get delivered together at the next stop.
IntroPage.2ou2i1u3: Of course, instead of packages we're sending ETH. And instead of waiting for the next train, we're waiting at most 12 seconds for our transactions to go through.
IntroPage.0im508u0: But why does it take 12 seconds at all ? Why isn't it instant ?
IntroPage.jbenm6yx: It's because of something called <Vocab>block time</Vocab>. On Ethereum, it takes about 12 seconds for the network to create a <Vocab>block</Vocab>.
IntroPage.4cud51dx: On average, it's probably closer to 6 seconds, so the animations you see are actually running at 2x speed. But don't worry about this too much.
IntroPage.0s9v6pnb: This "block" is what makes up the word "blockchain."
IntroPage.hs9vdihr: Think of a block like a train in the animation above. The train arrives on schedule, picks up everyone's transactions, then leaves for its destination.
IntroPage.oq8ddkdm: is an actual real-time visualization for the Ethereum network if you are curious.
IntroPage.3245z5hn: Let's say that you have to pay Alice, Bob, and Carol. All of them. Maybe they each took you out to dinner last week.
IntroPage.k02oslhh: Try sending each of them ETH. (The send button will automatically load the next recipient.)
IntroPage.eta03hnt: When we send out all these different transactions, they get collected into a <Vocab>block</Vocab>. So a block is a list of all the transactions that have happened. And a new block gets published around every 12 seconds.
IntroPage.1z1itoyu: Once we have more than one block, we have a <Vocab>blockchain</Vocab>. As the name suggests, it's a chain of blocks, or an ordered list of transactions.
IntroPage.vdukoicn: But what other types of transactions are there ? So far we've only seen sending and receiving ETH.
IntroPage.576s4xi9: In addition to sending ETH around, we can also interact with <Vocab>apps</Vocab> on the Ethereum network. These interactions are also transactions!
IntroPage.q024c9yz: What does that mean ? What does an app look like ?

AppsPage.pd5vqu9g: An app on Ethereum is a program that can also send or receive ETH
AppsPage.oxvj1gzg: In blockchain jargon, this type of program is called a
AppsPage.1hu6ukuz: What do these programs look like ?
AppsPage.g4or0b0l: What kinds of rules can we set ?
AppsPage.9mz5yoil: When will I stop with these hackneyed rhetorical questions ?
AppsPage.bsu1ceau: Okay, okay, let's get back to an example.
AppsPage.zc2jt1as: Remember that example earlier, where we had to pay Alice, Bob, and Carol one at a time ? Sending money to all three of them took several button clicks.
AppsPage.yhgsubcu: What if we could automate that to just one click ?
AppsPage.e6ztltqq: Let's look at a simplified smart contract
AppsPage.vvw8sv8l: This is a simplified example that doesn't use real code, of course. To learn more, check out
AppsPage.h8ew1xkg: , a programming language used to write smart contracts on Ethereum.
AppsPage.g2l6yzle: (If you haven't read or written code before, don't worry, just try to read the above text like a formal agreement, or a specific formula and see if it makes some sense.)
AppsPage.8jx1igub: ...in other words, it means whenever our Payment Splitter smart contract receives ETH, it'll automatically send the right proportion (1/3) to each person.
AppsPage.nyqa6lup: Now, we can use this simple program to send money to everyone at once, instead of individually sending everyone ETH one at a time.
AppsPage.3vq8r7vc: How do we run this program ?
AppsPage.b41xd9y3: On Ethereum, all smart contracts have their own address. To run this program, we just send ETH to its address. So it's a transaction, just like how sending ETH to Alice, Bob, or Carol is also a transaction.
AppsPage.pyplvmqd: Once the program receives ETH, it'll automatically do its job and split the funds three ways between Alice, Bob, and Carol as part of the same transaction.
AppsPage.3exvhrwg: Here, give it a try yourself.
AppsPage.fd2xeybr: Because the split amounts are coded up, it's also very easy to change them.
AppsPage.0exy4wpo: Let's say that Alice, Bob, and Carol all baked cookies for a bake sale.
AppsPage.9clig77r: Alice has baked half of all the cookies, and Bob and Carol each baked a quarter. Let's say they take sales in ETH so they tell everyone to send them money to a Payment Splitter smart contract.
AppsPage.n1e2bkp4: How can we change the Payment Splitter program to instead send 50% to Alice, 25% to Bob, and 25% to Carol ?
AppsPage.4jc9wthr: All we need to do is change the percentages we had for each person in our smart contract!
AppsPage.ir7ol0xy: We change the 33% for Alice to 50%, and the 33% for Bob and Carol to 25%.
AppsPage.cmdyl7hu: Now, when we send ETH to this new Payment Splitter, it automatically splits the funds 50/25/25 between Alice, Bob, and Carol.
AppsPage.0pgtzvrx: This is just the tip of the iceberg. There are many other types of smart contracts we could write to handle even more complex types of payments.
AppsPage.ot12zv6y: Change the split proportions (we already saw this one)
AppsPage.l6cgj2fm: Add or remove recipients (e.g. remove 👩‍🦰 Carol, or we could add 🕵️‍♀️ Eve)
AppsPage.t2pini1r: Charge a processing fee (e.g. send 1% to ourselves, then pass the rest along)
AppsPage.c14l0s25: Take in money from 2 people, and pay it out to 1 person (e.g. to settle a bet)
AppsPage.eg46p0ga: All of this can let us make very flexible and customizable programs to handle payments.
AppsPage.iwck0ypz: Let's go back to the bake sale example for a second. In an ideal world, we can sell cookies to people for ETH.
AppsPage.950d1qtc: In the real world, however, most people won't own ETH. They may not even know how to buy it. But almost everyone will have US Dollars in some shape or form (cash, credit, debit, etc.)
AppsPage.kkmj25ub: Can the Ethereum network handle dollars ?
AppsPage.xangcnuf: As I mentioned at the very beginning, we can use all sorts of currencies on the Ethereum network. Including digital dollars!

TokensPage.z8d0f7sy: A <Vocab>token</Vocab> is a currency that can be sent on a blockchain network.
TokensPage.q9zkaa3z: You can receive all types of tokens with the same
TokensPage.jl2dz2hg: address. There's no need to use a new account for each token type.
TokensPage.e7u5u0rj: All of our examples so far have used ETH. But on the Ethereum network, there are many, many different types of tokens.
TokensPage.rprepkgp: One important category of tokens are called
TokensPage.dzcbmaer: are tokens whose value is tied to a currency. Like I mentioned earlier, these include tokens which track the US Dollar (and we'll focus on them). But there are also ones that track other real world currencies like the Euro and even other assets like gold or silver!
TokensPage.jezfxs0e: Unlike ETH, which has a fluctuating price depending on market conditions, these USD stablecoins are always tracking the US Dollar. So 1 USDC or 1 USDT will always be redeemable for $1. This makes it great for payments, merchants, and finance.
TokensPage.k1xhwqp5: Under the hood, a company manages a stablecoin. These companies will put money into insured bank accounts or short-dated US treasuries. Then, for each $1 that they put in, they will
TokensPage.hy7k3t60: A physical mint will create new physical coins. In a similar way, a digital mint will create new digital tokens.
TokensPage.yzktxjr7: And how do our accounts keep track of everything ?
TokensPage.hgktl338: Imagine the Ethereum network contains a super big spreadsheet.
TokensPage.89ozdctc: This spreadsheet has tables for every token and every account ever created. For each token, there is a column for address and balance. This way, we can keep track of everyone's balances for every token.
TokensPage.yp8hkx14: This spreadsheet model helps us think about what it really means when we "send" a token to another address (whether it's a person or a smart contract).
TokensPage.9gyvbcuo: A "send" means updating the balance in the spreadsheet. The sender's balance goes down, and the receiver's balance goes up.
TokensPage.cc813yry: So if Alice sends Bob 10 USDC, we can think of the Ethereum network updating the spreadsheet cells for Alice and Bob's accounts.
TokensPage.obg0emhb: When Alice sends 10 USDC to Bob, their balances in the spreadsheet are updated.
TokensPage.jb8axe00: So when a stablecoin company <Vocab>mints</Vocab> tokens, they are sending a digital message to the Ethereum network to update the big spreadsheet so that their balance increases.
TokensPage.f07ji1p4: We can send tokens around on the Ethereum network.
TokensPage.2dpjh24a: But how do we actually get them "out" if we want to spend them somewhere else ?
TokensPage.zxk0qd25: If at any point you want to cash out, you can send the stablecoins in your wallet to one of these stablecoin companies, and they'll wire US Dollars back into your bank account. Many other fintech companies like Stripe or PayPal also support something similar. Under the hood, these companies will <Vocab>burn</Vocab> the tokens, and they'll transfer you the dollars.
TokensPage.ki366lip: As you may have guessed, <Vocab>burning</Vocab> is the opposite of minting. Instead of adding to someone's balance, we are now subtracting.
TokensPage.u3fcthvl: Okay so now we know we know about stablecoins and smart contracts.
TokensPage.a9ivk0qd: Together, we can build new types of apps!
TokensPage.slaxvdj7: What kinds of cooler stuff can we build ?
TokensPage.pc209rik: Let's do a deeper dive into smart contracts, now with tokens...

Apps2Page.kwu9h3c3: With stablecoins, we can now send dollars and transact in more familar ways.
Apps2Page.vqe06pdd: We've already covered how smart contracts can let us write different types of apps to handle payments, split bills, share fees, etc.
Apps2Page.u5g8j7qj: What happens when we combine them ?
Apps2Page.m0o2a5tk: Here, we'll cover more varied app types like:
Apps2Page.cjtczuqk: Earning Yield: how to earn interest on your dollars, similar to a high-yield savings account
Apps2Page.emq6yw9l: New Payment Methods: how we can support creators with new ways of paying
Apps2Page.u4njx859: Trading Markets: how to use stablecoins to buy ETH and vice versa
Apps2Page.7e44t3nr: As mentioned earlier, stablecoin companies will hold some of money in US Treasuries. This allows them to earn interest on their deposits and then pass those earnings back on to you.
Apps2Page.c6a4neai: Thus, there are apps that let you deposit your stablecoins to earn interest, around 4-6% APR.
Apps2Page.d1w0hqfc: You get the benefits of a savings account, and the convenience of being able to send your money around quickly 24/7.
Apps2Page.c3ybpklc: Another benefit is that interest on Ethereum is paid out every block, rather than needing to wait every month or every day.
